title: The Pelvis
question: Which bone is glowing?
lines: Five vertebrae fused into one bone. Can you name it?
We're looking at the pelvis from behind.
Which bone is glowing?
The coccyx is the small tail below it, not this triangle.
This triangular bone wedges between the two hip bones.
It's B. The sacrum.
Why it matters: it links your spine to the pelvis.

title: The Pelvis
question: What's its everyday name?
lines: Humans lost their tails, but this small bone remains.
Watch the small bone at the very bottom of the spine.
What's the everyday name of this bone?
The sitting bone is part of the hip bone, off to each side.
This one is a few small fused vertebrae below the sacrum.
It's C. The tailbone, or coccyx.
Why it matters: pelvic floor muscles and ligaments attach to it.

title: The Pelvis
question: Which side of the patient is it?
lines: The pelvis is built from matching left and right halves.
Watch the glowing hip bone on one side.
Which side of the patient is it?
Seen from the front, the patient's right is on our left.
So the glowing bone is on the patient's right.
It's A. The patient's right.
Why it matters: anatomy uses the patient's left and right.

title: The Pelvis
question: Which vertebra sits on the sacrum?
lines: One small back bone rests right on top of the pelvis.
Watch the glowing bone just above the sacrum.
Which vertebra sits on the sacrum?
L3 is higher up in the low back.
The last lumbar vertebra is L5, and it joins the sacrum.
It's D. L5, the fifth lumbar vertebra.
Why it matters: it is the link between the spine and the pelvis.

title: The Pelvis
question: Each hip bone is how many fused bones?
lines: You were born with more bones than you have now. Here's one.
Watch the two big glowing hip bones.
Each hip bone is how many fused bones?
The ilium, ischium and pubis fuse as you grow.
That's three bones in each hip bone.
It's B. Three.
Why it matters: it explains why the hip bone has three named parts.

title: The Pelvis
question: Which bones hold the thighbone's ball?
lines: Your thighbone meets the pelvis at a ball-and-socket joint.
Watch the two big bones glowing at the sides.
Which bones hold the thighbone's ball?
The sacrum sits between them at the back, not at the sides.
Each glowing bone has a deep socket for the ball.
It's B. The hip bones.
Why it matters: this ball and socket lets the leg swing in a wide circle.

title: The Pelvis
question: Which two bones are glowing?
lines: Your spine doesn't end at your lower back. It ends here.
Watch the glowing bones at the back of the pelvis.
Which two bones are glowing?
L4 and L5 are lumbar vertebrae, which sit above them.
The wide triangle is the sacrum. The small tip is the coccyx.
It's C. The sacrum and coccyx.
Why it matters: together they close the back of the pelvic ring.

title: The Pelvis
question: What do these bones form?
lines: A bony bowl sits at the base of your spine. What is it called?
Watch the glowing bones at your hips.
What do these bones form?
The shoulder girdle is at the top of the body. This is at the bottom.
It's A. The pelvic girdle.
Why it matters: it carries the upper body and links the spine to the legs.

title: The Pelvis
question: Which bones are at your hips?
lines: Put your hands on your hips. Which bones are you touching?
Watch the two large glowing bones.
Which bones are at your hips?
The lowest ribs sit higher up. These wide, flaring bones sit lower.
It's D. The hip bones.
Why it matters: the thighbones fit into them, so they carry your weight.
